validated_results.title: Coffee consumption and bladder cancer risk.
validated_results.reason: Original hospital-based case-control study in northern Italy reporting a multivariate relative risk for tea drinking and incident bladder cancer.

extraction.population: Cases and controls from two areas of northern Italy

sample_size.excerpt: The relation between consumption of regular and decaffeinated coffee and other methylxanthine-containing beverages and bladder cancer was analysed in a case-control study in two different areas of northern Italy (555 cases and 855 controls).
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 555 + 855 = 1410

cases.excerpt: The relation between consumption of regular and decaffeinated coffee and other methylxanthine-containing beverages and bladder cancer was analysed in a case-control study in two different areas of northern Italy (555 cases and 855 controls).

effect_size.excerpt: The RR was 1.2 for one cup of coffee per day, 1.4 for two, 1.5 for three and 1.4 for four or more (P = 0.05). RRs for current drinkers were 1.5 (0.9-2.4) for decaffeinated coffee, 0.9 (0.6-1.2) for tea, and 0.6 (0.3-1.4) for cola.

confidence_interval.excerpt: The multivariate relative risk (RR) adjusted for smoking, occupation and sociodemographic variables for coffee drinkers versus non-drinkers was 1.3 (95% CI 1.0-1.8). The RR was 1.2 for one cup of coffee per day, 1.4 for two, 1.5 for three and 1.4 for four or more (P = 0.05).
